title: Champagne, Chalk to Cork
subRegion: Reims, Épernay, Côte des Blancs and Côte des Bar

bestPeriod.note: Late September into October is harvest (vendange), the region is at its most alive, but book grande marque cellar tours further ahead.

summary: A week from Reims' Roman chalk cellars to Épernay's Avenue de Champagne and the grower villages of the Côte des Blancs and Côte des Bar.
hook: Under Reims and Épernay run more than a hundred kilometres of chalk galleries, some dug by the Romans, all cool and dark enough to age a wine for decades undisturbed, the UNESCO-listed "Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars." This week works from the grande marque crayères of Reims through the Avenue de Champagne to the grower villages of the Côte des Blancs, then south to the quieter, Pinot Noir-driven Côte des Bar, with the RM-versus-NM distinction as the thread that ties it together.

snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 140 km by train and car across the week; flat town walking, gently rolling vineyard paths in the Côte des Blancs
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG); TGV from CDG-2 direct to Reims, approx. 45 min
snapshot.Who It Suits: Wine drinkers ready to book grande marque tours weeks ahead and take a full day for the quieter Aube

itinerary.title: Reims, cathedral first
itinerary.morning: Fly into CDG and take the direct TGV to Reims, about 45 minutes from the airport station. Walk straight to Notre-Dame de Reims, the coronation cathedral of French kings, and look for the Chagall windows in the axial chapel.
itinerary.afternoon: Settle into central Reims and walk the streets around Place Drouet d'Erlon, the city's main dining artery.
itinerary.evening: Dinner built around jambon de Reims (a cooked, herbed ham specific to the city) and a glass of grande marque Champagne by the glass, an easy, low-commitment introduction before the cellar visits start.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 5. Approx. tasting spend: €18, €25.

itinerary.title: Into the crayères
itinerary.morning: Reservation tour at Veuve Clicquot or Pommery, both age Champagne in Roman-era chalk pits (crayères) beneath Reims, and neither takes walk-ins; book online several weeks ahead, especially for weekend slots. Pommery's cellars are the more theatrical of the two, with contemporary art installed among the galleries.
itinerary.afternoon: If your week lands on a Wednesday, Friday or Saturday, the covered Halles du Boulingrin market runs its morning session, a restored Art Deco hall worth the detour.
itinerary.evening: Fossier, the biscuiterie that has made the biscuit rose de Reims since 1756, keeps a shop in town; buy a box and eat one dipped in a glass of Champagne after dinner, the traditional way it's served locally.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 6. Approx. tasting spend: €35, €55.

itinerary.title: Taittinger, and south to Épernay
itinerary.morning: A second Reims crayère tour, at Taittinger, partly built into the cellars of the old Saint-Nicaise abbey, some sections 13th-century. Book online in advance; same-day availability is rare in season.
itinerary.afternoon: Train to Épernay, about 25 minutes on the regional line. Check into your base for the next four nights and walk the Avenue de Champagne, the single street where Moët & Chandon, Mercier, Perrier-Jouët and de Castellane all keep their headquarters above more than 100 km of combined cellars.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Épernay: andouillette if you want the local specialty in full, or a gentler potée champenoise (a slow-cooked pork and vegetable stew) if not.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2 (Reims). Km travelled: 30. Approx. tasting spend: €45, €65.

itinerary.title: The Avenue, properly
itinerary.morning: Reservation tour at Moët & Chandon, the largest house on the avenue and the most tour-ready, book online well ahead for a specific time slot, since capacity per day is genuinely limited despite the scale of the operation.
itinerary.afternoon: De Castellane, further down the avenue, keeps a walk-in-friendly visitor centre built around its own tower, climb it for a rooftop view over Épernay before the cellar visit. Mercier, next door, still runs a version of its historic laser-guided electric train through the cellars; check current booking requirements online, as reservation policy shifts by season.
itinerary.evening: Dinner with chaource, the soft, bloomy-rind cheese from the Aube, as a preview of Day 6.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2. Km travelled: 4. Approx. tasting spend: €50, €70.

itinerary.title: Hautvillers and the Côte des Blancs
itinerary.morning: Bus or taxi to Hautvillers, the hilltop village where Dom Pérignon is buried in the abbey church, the myth of Champagne's invention is overstated, but the abbey and the village's painted wrought-iron shop signs (each depicting a different Champagne-related trade) are genuinely worth the half-day.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive or taxi south into the Côte des Blancs, Cramant, Avize, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Chardonnay country and the source of blanc de blancs. Look at any bottle's small print for the producer code: RM (récoltant-manipulant) means a grower who grows the grapes and makes the wine themselves; NM (négociant-manipulant) means a house that buys in grapes, which covers most of the grande marque names visited earlier this week.
itinerary.evening: Reservation tasting at Pierre Péters in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger or Agrapart & Fils in Avize, both long-established grower estates, email a few weeks ahead, since these are small operations without a dedicated visitor programme, and expect to buy a bottle or two rather than just taste and leave.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 35. Approx. tasting spend: €25, €40.

itinerary.title: South to the Côte des Bar
itinerary.morning: This is the long day. Drive or take the train (Épernay-Troyes, changing if needed, roughly 1h30-2h) into the Aube département, the Côte des Bar, a Pinot Noir-heavy sub-region far enough from Reims and Épernay that it sees a fraction of the visitors.
itinerary.afternoon: Reservation visit at Drappier in Urville, a long-established grower house that has farmed the same site since the 18th century, email ahead, and expect a warmer, less scripted welcome than the grande marque tours earlier in the week. If time allows, drive on to Les Riceys, the only commune in France permitted to produce three separate appellations (Champagne, Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys still wine).
itinerary.evening: Dinner nearby built around chaource at its actual source, alongside a Côte des Bar Champagne, almost entirely Pinot Noir, rounder and less mineral than Côte des Blancs bottlings.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 200 (round trip). Approx. tasting spend: €25, €35.

itinerary.title: Last glass, and out
itinerary.morning: Back in Épernay, a final walk down the Avenue de Champagne for any house you didn't reach, or a return visit to buy bottles directly from a producer you liked earlier in the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Train to Paris (TGV via Reims or direct regional connections, roughly 1h30-2h total) or back to CDG for the flight home.
itinerary.evening: Departure, or a final night in Paris if your flight is early the next morning.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 140. Approx. tasting spend: €20, €40 (bottle purchases).

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel near Place Drouet d'Erlon
accommodationStrategy.description: Walking distance to the cathedral, the crayère visitor entrances, and the station for the short hop to Épernay, the right base for the Reims-focused first nights.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel on or near the Avenue de Champagne
accommodationStrategy.description: Puts you inside walking distance of Moët, Mercier and de Castellane, with taxis and rental pickup easy to arrange for the Côte des Blancs and Côte des Bar days.

accommodationStrategy.name: A chambre d'hôtes in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger or Cramant
accommodationStrategy.description: An alternative for the middle of the week if you'd rather be inside grower-Champagne country than commuting to it; several growers rent rooms above or beside their own cellars.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; also 15 (SAMU medical), 17 (police), 18 (fire) work directly in France.
logistics.bookingWindows: Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, Pommery and Taittinger require online reservation weeks ahead, especially for weekends; walk-up availability is rare in season. De Castellane and Mercier are the most walk-in-friendly of the well-known houses, though booking is still recommended.
logistics.money: Cards are accepted everywhere in Reims and Épernay; smaller growers in the Aube may prefer cash for round-number purchases.

other.label: Booking grower estates
other.text: Email 3-4 weeks ahead for Pierre Péters, Agrapart or Drappier; these are small teams without a dedicated booking office, and a purchase after tasting is the expected norm rather than an option.

other.label: Drink-drive alternative
other.text: Do not rent a car for the Reims-Épernay core of the trip; TER trains connect them in about 25 minutes. For the Côte des Blancs and Côte des Bar, hire a local driver through the Épernay tourist office, or rent a car and appoint a strict non-drinking driver for those two days only.

other.label: Cycling option
other.text: Signed vineyard cycling loops run out of Épernay and Hautvillers for a lower-key alternative to a car on the Côte des Blancs day.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Halles du Boulingrin in Reims runs Wednesday, Friday and Saturday mornings only, plan around it rather than assuming a daily market.

proTips: Learn RM versus NM before Day 5; once you can read the two letters on a label, every Champagne shelf in France reads differently.
Book Moët & Chandon and one crayère tour (Pommery or Veuve Clicquot) on different days, not back to back, both run 60-90 minutes and stacking them dulls the second visit.
Climb the de Castellane tower before, not after, its cellar tour, the light is better in late morning and the queue is shorter.
On the Côte des Blancs day, taste Cramant, Avize and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger back to back if you can arrange more than one grower stop; the chalk-driven minerality shifts noticeably village to village.
The Côte des Bar day rewards an early start, Drappier's morning slots are quieter, and it leaves time for Les Riceys without rushing the drive back.
Buy biscuit rose de Reims at the Fossier shop itself rather than a supermarket version; the texture difference is real, and it's the one local product built specifically to eat with Champagne.

packingNotes: A light jacket for the crayères and cellars, chalk galleries run a constant 10-12°C year-round.
Comfortable shoes for cobbled town streets and the Avenue de Champagne's long blocks.
A soft wine bag or case box for bottles bought at Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Avize or Drappier.
Smart-casual layers for grande marque tastings, which run more formal than a village cellar.
A phrasebook or app; Reims and Épernay are tourist-fluent in English, but the Aube less so.
A printed copy of tour confirmations for houses that check names against a booking list at the door.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A grande marque tour is sold out.** Book the moment your dates are fixed; if you're shut out, De Castellane and Mercier usually have shorter lead times than Moët, Veuve Clicquot or Taittinger.
**The Côte des Bar day runs long and you miss dinner reservations.** Build a two-hour buffer into the return drive or train; the Aube connections are less frequent than the Reims-Épernay core.

**A grower estate doesn't reply to your email.** The Épernay tourist office (Maison du Champagne / Office de Tourisme) keeps an updated list of growers currently welcoming visitors and can suggest an alternative in the same village.
**Rain washes out the Hautvillers or Côte des Blancs walking.** Cellars absorb a wet day easily; shift the vineyard walking to Day 7 morning if the forecast clears.
